extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, and media/journalism practitioners interested in Stern magazine and German news magazines
extracted.subtask_description: Historical and descriptive guidance about Stern's editorial approach and journalistic practices — e.g., its 'nutzwertiger Journalismus' (useful journalism), investigative emphasis, visual design choices, and provocative cover strategy. Useful for understanding the magazine's publishing standards and tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: nutzwertiger Journalismus ('useful journalism')
rubrics_metrics.description: The emphasis is on providing sufficient background on topic to allow readers opportunity to arrive at their own judgements rather than have these decided for them editorially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains Stern's editorial philosophy: give context and background so readers can form judgments. Implicitly values explanatory reporting over purely opinionated headlines; this principle shaped article length and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longer and investigative articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles tended to be longer and more investigative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stern pursued in-depth reportage and investigative pieces. This is presented as a quality characteristic distinguishing it from more tabloid rivals; suitable for topics requiring background and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad topic selection including social and lifestyle issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguished from similarly directed Der Spiegel by the wider range of social and life-style issues covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial scope includes not only hard political news but also social and lifestyle topics; this breadth is part of Stern's identity and affects choices of subject matter and audience positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater reliance on illustration and graphic design
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguished ... by a greater reliance of illustration and graphic design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual presentation is a deliberate editorial dimension: strong photography, graphics and layout are used to complement and distinguish reporting. This influences story packaging and reader engagement strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to challenge political and social conventions (break taboos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stern was open to the questioning, from a liberal and left perspective, of the post-war political and social order in West Germany; willing to break the relative post-war silence on the National-Socialist past and to publish taboo-breaking pieces (e.g., 'We've had abortions!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial stance supports investigative and critical coverage of established powers and taboos. Producing such content may provoke controversy but is framed as part of the magazine's mission to question consensus and stimulate public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of provocative cover imagery and headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Stern generated cover-page controversy (e.g., photo-shopped Trump as giving a Nazi salute, 'Sein Kampf'); covers have been used to visualise strong editorial arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers are used as a rhetorical device to provoke discussion and signal editorial positions. Editors should weigh impact: such imagery can attract attention but also draw harsh criticism (domestic and international) and accusations of trivialising historical atrocities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism; maintain editorial safeguards (vetting and credibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hitler Diaries fiasco showed the hazards of 'sensation-seeking check book journalism' and led to resignations and a loss of credibility; staff protested management bypassing traditional editorial channels and safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete anti-pattern: paying for and publishing unvetted sensational material undermines credibility. Guidance implied: enforce strong editorial verification processes, preserve traditional editorial checks, and prioritize source reliability to protect reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations about sexualised imagery and dignity of subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine's frequent 'cover girls' were challenged as denying the human dignity of women by presenting them 'as a mere sexual object' (legal action initiated in 1978).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial use of nudes/sexualised photography can attract feminist and public critique and even legal challenges; editors must consider issues of dignity, objectification, and potential accusations of sexism or racism when commissioning imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation of print format to mimic online features
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2013 reformatting of the printed edition mimics on-line features and conventions: greater use of sidebars and infographics, less formal language, and even greater emphasis on arresting large-print photography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and language changes to bridge print and digital audiences: adopt online conventions in print to increase immediacy and visual engagement. This implies editorial choices toward shorter, scannable elements (sidebars, infographics) and a more conversational tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and expand online/e-paper presence while recognizing differences between copies sold and actual readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Stern has had an on-line presence since 1995; e-paper circulation increased from ~8,500 in Q2 2015 to ~26,800 in Q4 2020. Actual readership is several times higher than copies sold or subscribed to online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial and business planning should account for digital distribution growth and the gap between circulation numbers and real audience reach. Strategies should track e-paper and online metrics and consider audience engagement beyond paid circulation.
